articles.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
articles.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.
articles.content:
A new Australian study suggests that zoo lions behave more like their wild counterparts when they are given whole animal carcasses as part of a feast and fast feeding schedule.

Published in Applied Animal Behaviour Science, the research was conducted by Adelaide University and Monarto Safari Park in South Australia. Scientists studied a group of adult male African lions after animal care staff added whole carcasses every nine days to an existing feeding routine designed around periods of eating and fasting.

Continuous video monitoring over three months showed that the lions spent much more time eating when carcasses were provided, rested for longer afterward, and gradually became more active as the fasting period continued. Together, these patterns more closely resembled the natural feeding cycles seen in wild lions.

Lead author Lesia Hryhorenko from Adelaide University's School of Animal and Veterinary Sciences said the study provides new information about how feeding routines can shape the behavior of carnivores living in human care.

"Wild lions don't eat at the same time every day. They experience natural periods of feasting and fasting depending on hunting success," Hryhorenko said.

"We wanted to understand how African lions in human care respond when feeding routines more closely resemble those natural patterns."

Tracking Lions Around the Clock

The research team - which included visiting Belgium Masters student Florence Demoulin from the University of Liege - observed three adult male lions at Monarto Safari Park before and after whole carcasses were introduced.

During the experimental phase, the three lions received approximately 200 kilograms of carcasses. The food was left available for as long as three days, after which the lions entered a period of rest and digestion.

Researchers used eight infrared cameras to record the animals continuously. This produced one of the most detailed 24 hour datasets yet assembled for African lions in human care under a carcass feeding regime.

The difference on carcass feeding days was substantial. The lions spent almost three times as long eating as they typically did. They also fed more frequently and for longer stretches as they tore apart, pulled at, manipulated, and consumed the carcasses.

These activities gave the animals more opportunities to perform the kinds of feeding behaviors that are part of life in the wild.

A Natural Feast and Fast Rhythm

Once the lions had finished feeding, they spent considerably more time lying down and resting. As the fasting period went on, their movement gradually increased again.

This repeating pattern of intense feeding, extended rest, and rising activity closely matched the feast and fast rhythm documented among wild lion populations.

"Providing whole carcasses changes much more than the nutritional content of the diet," Hryhorenko said.

"It gives lions the opportunity to engage in behaviors such as tearing, pulling and manipulating food over extended periods, which are important components of their natural feeding ecology."

Pacing Appears Linked to Routine, Not Hunger

The researchers also tracked pacing, a repetitive behavior in carnivores that is often linked to anticipation.

Pacing increased slightly over the study period, but it did not consistently rise as the lions went longer without food. Instead, the largest increases occurred around predictable events such as keeper arrivals and times when the animals were moved between areas of their habitat.

That pattern suggests pacing may have been more strongly connected to familiar daily routines and the expectation of feeding than to hunger itself.

The researchers also found no increase in aggression or disruption to the lions' social stability during whole carcass feeding events.

Co-author Associate Professor Alexandra Whittaker said the findings demonstrate why animal behavior needs to be monitored over longer periods when researchers evaluate zoo management practices.

"Many zoo studies focus only on what happens immediately after food is provided," Associate Professor Whittaker said.

"Our results show that feeding schedules can influence behavior for days afterwards, making it essential to look at behavioral patterns across the entire feeding cycle rather than a single feeding event."

The researchers say future work could combine behavioral monitoring with physiological measurements to provide a more complete picture of how different feeding strategies affect animal welfare and well-being.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a meaningful scientific study that improves the welfare and natural behavior of lions in human care by changing their feeding routines to mimic wild patterns. This has broad implications for animal welfare in zoos globally, providing measurable benefits to the animals' quality of life and behavioral health. The study is detailed and focused on a single topic with clear positive impact.
articles.personality_title: Changing zoo lions’ feeding to whole carcasses brings out natural behavior
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Lions in zoos often eat on a fixed schedule with prepared food, which can differ from how they eat in the wild. Wild lions eat whole prey and have periods of feasting and fasting based on hunting success.

**What happened** – Scientists in Australia studied three adult male African lions at Monarto Safari Park. They added whole animal carcasses to the lions’ feeding routine every nine days, instead of daily meals. Cameras recorded the lions’ behavior continuously for three months to see how they responded.

**Impact** – The lions spent nearly three times longer eating when given whole carcasses. They tore apart and manipulated the food, which is more like wild lions’ natural behavior. After eating, the lions rested more and then became gradually more active during fasting, showing a natural feast and fast rhythm. This change improved their feeding behavior without causing more aggression or social problems.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to combine behavior tracking with health measurements to understand how feeding changes affect lions’ overall well-being. This method could help improve care for other carnivores in zoos by encouraging natural behaviors.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Feeding zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule helps them act more like wild lions, improving their natural behavior and welfare.
articles.personality_title_fr: Donner des carcasses entières aux lions de zoo révèle leur comportement naturel
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les lions en zoo mangent souvent selon un horaire fixe avec de la nourriture préparée, ce qui diffère de leur alimentation sauvage. Dans la nature, les lions mangent des proies entières et alternent entre périodes de festin et de jeûne selon leurs succès de chasse.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques australiens ont étudié trois lions mâles adultes au parc safari Monarto. Ils ont ajouté des carcasses entières à leur routine alimentaire tous les neuf jours, au lieu de repas quotidiens. Des caméras ont filmé leur comportement en continu pendant trois mois.

**Impact** – Les lions ont passé presque trois fois plus de temps à manger avec des carcasses entières. Ils ont déchiré et manipulé la nourriture, ce qui ressemble davantage au comportement naturel des lions sauvages. Après avoir mangé, ils se reposaient plus longtemps puis devenaient progressivement plus actifs pendant le jeûne, montrant un rythme naturel de festin et de jeûne. Ce changement a amélioré leur comportement sans augmenter l’agressivité ou les problèmes sociaux.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent combiner l’observation comportementale avec des mesures de santé pour mieux comprendre l’effet de l’alimentation sur le bien-être des lions. Cette méthode pourrait aider à améliorer le soin des autres carnivores en zoo en favorisant leurs comportements naturels.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Donner des carcasses entières aux lions de zoo selon un rythme de festin et de jeûne les aide à se comporter comme des lions sauvages, améliorant leur comportement naturel et leur bien-être.
articles.personality_title_es: Cambiar la alimentación de los leones en zoológicos con presas enteras despierta su comportamiento natural
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los leones en zoológicos suelen comer con horarios fijos y alimentos preparados, diferente a su alimentación en la naturaleza. Los leones salvajes comen presas enteras y tienen períodos de festín y ayuno según su éxito en la caza.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en Australia estudiaron a tres leones machos adultos en el Parque Safari Monarto. Añadieron presas enteras a su rutina de alimentación cada nueve días, en lugar de comidas diarias. Usaron cámaras para grabar el comportamiento de los leones durante tres meses.

**Impacto** – Los leones pasaron casi tres veces más tiempo comiendo con las presas enteras. Desgarraban y manipulaban la comida, comportándose más como leones salvajes. Después de comer, descansaban más y luego se volvían gradualmente más activos durante el ayuno, mostrando un ritmo natural de festín y ayuno. Este cambio mejoró su comportamiento sin aumentar la agresión o problemas sociales.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean combinar el monitoreo del comportamiento con mediciones de salud para entender mejor cómo la alimentación afecta el bienestar de los leones. Este método podría ayudar a mejorar el cuidado de otros carnívoros en zoológicos fomentando sus comportamientos naturales.

**Resumen en una frase** – Alimentar a los leones de zoológico con presas enteras en un ciclo de festín y ayuno les ayuda a actuar más como leones salvajes, mejorando su comportamiento natural y bienestar.

articles.title: Neanderthal Europe was as much a wooden age as a stone age
articles.summary: When Neanderthals dominated Europe, it was likely that wood was at least as important to them as stone for working into tools
articles.content:
When Neanderthals dominated Europe, it was likely that wood was at least as important to them as stone for working into tools

A wooden object from the Abric Romaní site interpreted as a wooden club Gerard Campeny/IPHES-CERCA

Wooden tools, weapons, building materials and domestic items discovered in a Spanish cave challenge the assumption that Neanderthals’ technological life was based primarily on stone.

The finds have given an unprecedented glimpse into everyday Neanderthal life and are a rare opportunity to recover part of their missing world, says Josep Vallverdú at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution in Spain.

“Neanderthal technology was not only made of stone; it was also made of wood,” he says.

Advertisement

“The archaeological record gives us a very biased picture of prehistoric technology. We see the stone because it survives, while a huge part of their material culture has simply disappeared.”

Vallverdú and his colleagues have now completed the first systematic review of nearly 600 wooden objects, all between 40,000 and 62,000 years old.

The finds have been collected by generations of archaeologists since the 1980s, excavated at a rock shelter site called Abric Romaní near Barcelona. They include timber imprints in travertine – a rock rich in calcium carbonate that precipitates out of water in certain environments. The rock preserves the patterns of the wood grain even though the timber long ago rotted away. Charred artefacts and actual preserved timber have also been found at the site.

Humans: The evolution of a species See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026 Find out more

The researchers’ first job was to determine exactly which pieces were used or made by Neanderthals. Only 13 qualified. Most of the remainder consist of trunks, branches, twigs, roots and firewood accumulations.

Maria Gema Chacón, also at the Catalan Institute, says the researchers have been surprised at how “complex Neanderthal woodworking could be, and how well they understood the properties of wood”, with the two spears being especially striking to her.

“Producing long, straight shafts and shaping them deliberately into pointed weapons required planning, skill and careful selection of the raw material,” says Chacón.

The technological behaviours preserved at Abric Romaní are comparable to those documented for Homo sapiens, she says.

Other finds included a mysterious wooden tripod, as well as timber trays reminiscent, in terms of likely utility, of the coolamons traditionally used by Indigenous Australians to carry food and water. Some of the wooden objects appear to be structural poles.

But perhaps the item that has most surprised the team is a “club-like” object that has no precedent from any other palaeolithic site.

Palmira Saladié, also at the Catalan Institute, says the club-like object is “not simply a stick with a thicker end”.

“There is a distinct narrow handle and an enlarged, asymmetrical head, giving the object a much more complex and deliberate form,” she says. “This particular configuration is what we have not been able to find a convincing parallel for in the prehistoric record.”

Vallverdú says the site shows that wood was a normal and important part of Neanderthals’ everyday life.

“We have evidence of woodworking across many archaeological levels and over thousands of years, and the objects are associated with very different activities: hunting, domestic tasks, containers and the organisation of living spaces,” he says.

Chris Stringer at the Natural History Museum in London says the archaeological record of wooden artefacts has been “severely constrained” by the generally poor preservation of organic materials.

The finds reveal a much wider technological repertoire of woodworking skills, he says.

“This is of course evidence from only one site, in one area, and one time span,” says Stringer, “so it’s just the tip of the iceberg in terms of a whole and mostly hidden technology that ran in parallel with the much better-known stone tools of the Palaeolithic.”

“Wood, plant fibres, hides, bone and other organic materials must have been central to daily life, but they normally disappear,” says Mariana Nabais, also at the Catalan Institute. “So when a site like Abric Romaní preserves wooden imprints and charred wooden objects, it is almost like suddenly seeing the missing half of the toolkit.”

Naoki Morimoto at Kyoto University in Japan describes the wooden objects as “remarkable”.

“Preserved organic materials are truly rare, and they reveal a ‘hidden’ aspect of Neanderthals that we have been missing,” says Morimoto.
articles.reasoning: The article reveals a significant archaeological discovery that broadens understanding of Neanderthal technology and daily life, showing that wood was as important as stone. This challenges previous assumptions and provides meaningful insights into human evolution and prehistoric technology, benefiting the general public's knowledge of history and anthropology.
articles.personality_title: New discoveries show Neanderthals used wood as much as stone for tools
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For a long time, scientists thought Neanderthals, early humans who lived in Europe, mainly used stone to make their tools and weapons. Wood and other materials have rarely been found because they usually decay over time.

**What happened** – Researchers studying a cave near Barcelona, Spain, called Abric Romaní, found nearly 600 wooden objects between 40,000 and 62,000 years old. These include wooden spears, a club-like weapon, trays, and structural poles. Only 13 of these were clearly made or used by Neanderthals, but they show careful shaping and skill.

**Impact** – This discovery changes how we understand Neanderthal life. It shows they were skilled at working with wood, not just stone. Making wooden spears with pointed ends took planning and knowledge of wood’s properties. The finds give a fuller picture of their daily lives, including hunting and building, which was hidden before because wood usually rots away.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue studying wooden tools from other sites to see if Neanderthals used wood as widely elsewhere. This may lead to a better understanding of how early humans lived and how their technology developed over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New evidence from Spain reveals that Neanderthals skillfully used wood alongside stone, broadening our view of their technology and daily life.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles découvertes montrent que les Néandertaliens utilisaient le bois autant que la pierre pour leurs outils
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Pendant longtemps, les scientifiques ont pensé que les Néandertaliens, des humains anciens vivant en Europe, utilisaient principalement la pierre pour fabriquer leurs outils et armes. Le bois et d'autres matériaux se retrouvent rarement car ils se décomposent avec le temps.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs étudiant une grotte près de Barcelone, en Espagne, appelée Abric Romaní, ont trouvé près de 600 objets en bois datant de 40 000 à 62 000 ans. Parmi eux, des lances en bois, une arme ressemblant à une massue, des plateaux et des poteaux de construction. Seuls 13 objets ont clairement été fabriqués ou utilisés par les Néandertaliens, mais ils montrent un travail soigné et des compétences.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change notre compréhension de la vie des Néandertaliens. Elle montre qu'ils savaient travailler le bois, pas seulement la pierre. Fabriquer des lances en bois avec des pointes demandait de la planification et une bonne connaissance du bois. Ces objets donnent une image plus complète de leur vie quotidienne, y compris la chasse et la construction, ce qui était caché auparavant car le bois se dégrade.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier les outils en bois d'autres sites pour voir si les Néandertaliens utilisaient aussi largement le bois ailleurs. Cela pourrait améliorer notre compréhension de la vie des premiers humains et de l'évolution de leur technologie.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De nouvelles preuves d'Espagne montrent que les Néandertaliens utilisaient habilement le bois en plus de la pierre, élargissant notre vision de leur technologie et de leur vie quotidienne.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos hallazgos muestran que los neandertales usaban la madera tanto como la piedra para sus herramientas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos pensaron que los neandertales, humanos antiguos que vivieron en Europa, usaban principalmente piedra para hacer sus herramientas y armas. La madera y otros materiales rara vez se encuentran porque suelen descomponerse con el tiempo.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores que estudiaron una cueva cerca de Barcelona, España, llamada Abric Romaní, encontraron casi 600 objetos de madera con edades entre 40,000 y 62,000 años. Estos incluyen lanzas de madera, un arma parecida a un garrote, bandejas y postes estructurales. Solo 13 objetos fueron claramente hechos o usados por neandertales, pero muestran un trabajo cuidadoso y habilidad.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento cambia cómo entendemos la vida de los neandertales. Muestra que eran habilidosos trabajando la madera, no solo la piedra. Fabricar lanzas de madera con puntas requería planificación y conocimiento de las propiedades de la madera. Estas piezas dan una imagen más completa de su vida diaria, incluyendo la caza y la construcción, que antes estaba oculta porque la madera se descompone.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando herramientas de madera en otros sitios para ver si los neandertales usaban la madera igual de ampliamente en otros lugares. Esto puede ayudar a entender mejor cómo vivían los primeros humanos y cómo evolucionó su tecnología.

**Resumen en una frase** – Nuevas evidencias de España muestran que los neandertales usaban la madera junto a la piedra, ampliando nuestra visión de su tecnología y vida diaria.
